example.problem: AC advertisement: '5-year comprehensive warranty.' Customer finds later that key parts (compressor, battery) have 1-year warranty, and labor is extra. Customer paid ₹50,000 expecting 5-year peace of mind; now faces ₹15,000 repair after 2 years. Is the company liable?
example.solution: Yes. Warranty claims are determined by the advertised terms, not fine print that contradicts them. If the ad says '5-year comprehensive,' that's the consumer's reasonable expectation. Fine print that reduces it violates the Consumer Protection Act (unfair term). Remedy: Company must honor 5-year warranty on all parts, pay labor costs, and reimburse the customer's repair bill (₹15,000) + compensation (₹10,000 for inconvenience). This teaches companies to be honest in ads.

slides.inSimpleWords: Misleading ads that hide terms in fine print are illegal—the main claim (5-year warranty) is what consumers relied on, and companies must honor it.

slides.title: Your Rights as a Digital Consumer
slides.storyContext: Priya now buys most things online—clothes, food, electronics. Platforms (Amazon, Flipkart, Swiggy) set their own terms. She realizes: can a platform charge ₹100 'surge pricing' during peak hours? Can it ban sellers arbitrarily? Can it access her data? What are her rights in a digital marketplace?

points.label: Platform Accountability
points.text: E-commerce and food-delivery apps are businesses, subject to consumer laws. Surge pricing is allowed if disclosed clearly. Arbitrary bans of sellers must be justified. Data privacy is protected—apps can't sell your data without consent.

points.label: Digital Privacy Rights
points.text: Personal data (name, address, purchases, location) is protected. Apps must get consent for data collection, can't share with third parties without permission, and must delete data on request (except tax/legal records).

points.label: Disputes in Digital Markets
points.text: If a Flipkart seller sends a counterfeit item, the platform is held partially liable (must verify sellers). Flipkart must resolve the issue: refund, replacement, or compensation. Disputes are filed online, faster than going to consumer court.

points.label: Future Protections
points.text: India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act (2023) set stronger privacy rules. Platform monopolies are being investigated (e.g., Amazon's preference for its own brands). Regulations are evolving faster than before.

example.problem: A food-delivery app accesses your location 24/7 even when you're not using it (to show nearby restaurants). You didn't explicitly consent. Is this legal? What's the remedy?
example.solution: No. Data access beyond necessity violates privacy rights. Remedy: (1) Submit a complaint to Data Protection Authority (new government body), (2) demand the app delete unnecessary data, (3) seek compensation. Companies like Google and Meta face large fines (₹100+ crore) for such violations. As consumer, you have the right to be forgotten (demand deletion of your data).

slides.inSimpleWords: Digital platforms must protect your privacy, disclose terms clearly, and be accountable for seller frauds—don't assume 'online = unprotected.'

points.text: Six consumer rights: safety, information, choice, being heard, redressal, and education. These are legal—companies must respect them or face fines and criminal liability.
Right to safety: products must be safe and tested; defective or fake products must be recalled, and companies must compensate harm. Expired medicines, counterfeit drugs carry severe penalties.
Right to information: all fees, terms, expiry dates, warnings must be disclosed clearly—hidden charges and misleading ads are illegal.
Right to fair price: hoarding, price-gouging, and exploitation are violations. During emergencies, governments cap prices. Online hidden fees must be disclosed upfront.

Right to redressal: consumer courts provide fast justice (1-2 years). Burden of proof is on the company—if a product fails early, it's assumed to be defective. You can demand replacement, refund, or compensation.
